newsitem.title: NORWAY: FEATURE - Human rights champion Norway rapped for racism.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Human rights champion Norway rapped for racism.

text.p: Norway, proud of its reputation as a champion of human rights, has been stung by criticism that it is not fighting racism hard enough at home.

The European Council Commission against Racism and Intolerance suggested recently that Norway review its legislation against discrimination and take preventive measures against anti-Semitism and xenophobia on a local level.
Norway, where the Nobel Peace Prize is awarded every year, at first stamped the eight-page report :"Not for public release".
The Labour government, which said it did not want it released until later, declassified it last month only after pressure from the media and the human rights organisation Amnesty International.
"It is in itself a symptom that the government tried to keep the report a secret," said Jan Borgen, secretary general of Amnestry International in Norway.

"It is important that Norway, which has such a high profile in international humanitarian work, cleans up its own act. But we think too highly of ourselves. We have appointed ourselves as moral guardians. The danger is we will not be taken seriously abroad if we can't admit our own shortcomings," he told Reuters.
Ironically, it was at the initiative of former Norwegian prime minister Gro Harlem Brundtland that the European Council's Plan of Action on fighting racism in Europe was set in motion.
POLICE AND PROSECUTORS CRITICISED
The commission noted that Norwegian police and prosecutors had been criticised for setting aside reports of violations of the penal code concerning racial harassment and discrimination of immigrants.
"The enforcement of existing legal measures may not have been sufficiently strict and...it could be queried whether the laws are effective in ensuring equal rights," the report said.
It said most studies had shown a tendency lately towards an increase in intolerant attitudes, particularly among young people who are the target of extreme right-wing groups.
The Local Government ministry questioned the report and said it had been classified because it was a draft. "In general, the report is a bit thin," a statement said.
RARE CHALLENGE
Norway, which mediated the 1993 Israeli-Palestinian peace pact and is known for taking the moral high ground on many issues, seldom sees it's own human rights record challenged.

Oeyvind Johnsen, editor of the left-of-centre daily Arbeiderbladet, challenged it in his book "Good Norwegians" a few months ago. He accused the Labour government of having legitimised anti-foreigner attitudes by introducing a stricter immigration policy in the late 1980s.
Brundtland quickly denied the accusation and said the government had had to deal with an increase in asylum seekers.

Johnsen, whose wife is Chilean, said wealthy Norway had shed its humanitarian face to become "aggressive and discriminating" against foreigners living here. Immigrants were turned back at pubs and their children harassed in school, he said.

"This development is not typically Norwegian. It is a European phenomenon. But the effects of xenophobia are more crushing here in the North where homogenity is so much more dominating, generosity is less in evidence and ways of alternative living are fewer," he said.
LILLEHAMMER OLYMPICS

The sparsely populated state of Viking decendants has one of the most homogeneous populations in Europe. Only 50,000 immigrants, or about one percent of the 4.3 million inhabitants, come from Asia, Africa and other non-European ethnic areas.

But a concentration of Pakistani, Vietnamese and other nationals to Oslo's east side has caused concern among many citizens in a city which through history has had limited contact with foreigners because of its geographical isolation.
Johnsen said anti-foreigner sentiments hit a peak at the February 1994 Lillehammer Winter Olympics where flag-waving Norwegian fans watched the host nation dominate many events.
He said the Games "became the first ritual manifestation of the new Norwegian nationalism of the 1990s.

"The Lillehammer Olympic Games turned into a chauvinist orgy you have rarely seen in other Olympic host nations. It was a sentimental, cheering homage to ourselves as a people, shutting out others, nostalgic and so self-centered it became pathetic -- and a source of concern."
He said surveys showed suspicion of foreigners increased among Norwegians after the Games.
A few months later, in November 1994, isolationist and anti-foreigner sentiment ran high as Norwegians in a referendum smugly rejected membership of the European Union, he noted.
RENEWED ATTACK ON IMMIGRATION POLICIES

The right-wing Progress Party, which is represented in parliament, picked up 12.1 percent of the vote in local elections in 1995 on its anti-immigrant platform. It launched a renewed attack on immigration policies at a recent conference setting the stage for September's general election.
"We must not allow the royal kingdom to become a base for Moslem fundamentalists," a party spokesman told Norwegian radio.
Fewer than 3,000 mostly Third World refugees settled in Norway last year.

Right-wing extremist violence against immigrants is rare, but last month six skinheads shouting "Sieg Heil" attacked a home for asylum-seekers near Bodoe in northern Norway, beating up two foreigners, police said.
A television documentary seeking to confront neo-Nazi ideas said far-right extremist scene was made up of just 300 beer-drinking youngsters, including maybe 50 activists.

Supreme Court lawyer Erik Gjems-Onstad, a decorated World War Two resistance fighter against Norway'S Nazi occupiers, spoke out against what he called a multi-cultural society in an interview with the daily newspaper Aftenposten. He compared the immigration to the Nazi invasion of the country in 1940.
"You don't need tanks to take over Norway today. You can do it just as easily with baby prams," Gjems-Onstad said.
An Aftenposten editorial said the government's handling of the European Council criticism was an embarrassment.
"We must obviously take it seriously when the European Commission against racism and intolerance requests more measures by Norway in the fight against racism," Aftenposten said.
"What we really need is a thorough debate on xenophobia."
